thread_title: Remains of the  Hurricane Creek White site
breadcrumb: Remains of the  Hurricane Creek White site

posts.body_html:
The original site where S. leucophylla hurricane creek white used to exist in the wild was plowed and turned into a pine tree plantation. While I never saw the original site before it was destroyed, I had heard it was a huge field filled with plants! The original site had many normal S. leucophyllas, but a few plants displayed the blinding white traps that we are fortunate enough to have preserved in cultivation prior to the site being destroyed.

A lot of people probably are wondering, what does this site look like today, and is there anything left? Surprisingly, there is still a tiny little patch remaining to this day, but it is slowly being overgrown by the surrounding shrubs. Are there any super-white plants left? Sort of, but nothing like what we have in cultivation.

2 years ago when we first spotted this relic patch, there was a little opening in the shrubs (which were much shorter at the time) and you could walk in there and see quite a few plants. This little clearing had a decent amount of sunlight. As of 2013 (2 years later), that open patch is now filled with thick shrubs, and there's no way you can even attempt to walk in there! All of the plants that were once receiving decent light are now etiolated and shaded. Many only produced phyllodia.

Will this patch survive in the long run? IF a fire comes through, or someone clears up the shrubs consistently, this relic site can potentially last a long time. However, the landowners clearly aren't interested in preserving these plants, and as is, the site will likely persist for a few more years at best.

In the case of the S. rubra wherryi Chatom giant site, in 2004 (?), the population was in the same situation: they were heavily shaded by thick shrubs and struggling to survive. As of 2013, we didn't find a single Sarracenia in the original Chatom giant site. There were also gigantic S. psittacinas that used to grow there..these were also all gone. While I remain optimistic that the little hurricane creek patch may persist for a few more years, I remain skeptical that it will last through time.


Photos of what remains of the original hurricane creek white site. We're going to keep an eye on this site in the years to come for more updates, good or bad. It's damn hard to find, I'll tell you that much! Keep in mind, this used to be a field, but is now thick shrubs that eventually turn into a non-native forest (pine plantation) behind them:



You used to be able to walk in here:


Still, we did find an impressive hurricane creek white plant here and there:



Most of them, however, looked like regular leucos, or relative white regular plants:












They may be starving for light, but they sure aren't starving for insects!






In two years, this will likely turn into thick brush:





Actually, some beautiful and interesting plants are still alive:






you can tell this is a relative of hurricane creek white:



Decent hurricane creek white plant:






The dark green and contrasting white is what makes hurricane creek white so unique. Most other populations don't have that characteristic:

posts.body_html:
KE: That dark mass are piles and piles of love bugs. I did see a lot of the carpenter bees on my last trip in 2011, but this time, majority of the traps were filled with love bugs. They were the #1 prey, but it's probably because this year, the love bug population was so massive. When we were driving on the highway, love bugs were "raining" on the windshield, and there were so many "splatter" marks that it was hard to drive. I have a picture somewhere that I'll upload.

Everywhere you go in the wild, love bugs were so prevalent, they would land on you and some even bite! They're really nasty insects.

posts.body_html: Do you think the increasing numbers of trees and large shrubs is using water with a detrimental effect on the moisture level of the bog?
posts.body_text: Do you think the increasing numbers of trees and large shrubs is using water with a detrimental effect on the moisture level of the bog?

posts.body_html:
KE: interestingly enough, not really. There doesn't seem to be much competition for water in the South because there's so much of it in the "boggy" areas. Even when it's dry or hasn't rained in a while, a lot of these sites have these unique "underground creeks" that constantly flow and keep the sites hydrated. In fact, on what seems to be dry land, you'll see these mounds where crayfish live! It's really bizzare.


Here you go: love bug guts! The locals tell me their bodies are like acid and eat away the paint if you don't wash it off after a while:

posts.body_html:
These plants are in the middle of nowhere, right next to many square miles of pine plantations. Finding the owner of this site will be a challenge: how do you find out who owns 500+ acres of a pine plantation in the middle of nowhere, and how do you tell one parcel from the next? On the other hand, at another site, it was really easy to find the owners: the site was in their front yard, and we happen to be there when they were there.

I have a friend down in Alabama who is investigating if he can go to the hurricane creek white site and do some controlled burning (he's fully trained). I'm not sure if he's been successful in finding the owners though, but he has the nature conservancy's contact info, and everything necessary to save this site. Fingers crossed...even for him, it's a long drive though (Alabama isn't a small state).
-Mike

posts.body_html:
Some more photos of the relic hurricane creek white site. Unfortunately, we were only here for 7-8 minutes, and Damon/Axel had that "I just saw a ghost" look in their eyes. They heard gunshots in the background, and while I didn't hear anything until they mentioned it, it didn't concern me because it was so far away. These guys were already spooked from the previous day when we were actually shot at, so I convinced myself to be considerate of their feelings and We all left without any hesitation.

Long story short, many of the amazing plants that we saw weren't photographed, and we also saw some jaw-dropping Lilium catesbaeis here too! It was a very interesting variant that I unfortuately didn't get a chance to photograph.

Anyhow, here's some more photos to enjoy. In this first photo, parts of the site can technically expand so long as the surrounding vegetation doesn't colonize it first. Notice the leucophyllas in the background:



3 years ago, you could walk in here and see S. leucophylla growing. Today, there's still a bunch of plants underneath all that growth, but they're all heavily shaded and only producing phyllodia:


One plant here had enough light to produce a decent trap-can you spot it?



And now for the closeup shots. Remember, this population was acres in size and mostly had regular leucophyllas before it was almost completely destroyed:



Here we go, this one sorta looks like one of the HCW's we have in cultivation:



This photo is for Calen: a HCW clone D wannabe:


I think this is the same trap:



Another photo for Calen: notice how there's red veins in this clone. I bet this one can be solid white under different environmental conditions:




Traps were mostly empty at all of the dozens of sites we visited. I don't think this spider is stuck: he/she's probably lurking in there for some lunch:



A lot of them at this site looked like this:



Not the best phenotypes, but you can tell the quality genetics are there:




Damaged pitcher is still quite beautiful:



Last but not least, another reddish one:
